title: The Harness Grew Up: What Changed in Agent Engineering This Month
question: What changed this month in how AI agent harnesses are built, evaluated, and operated, and which of those developments matter most to practitioners?
argument: The month's most consequential developments share one theme: the harness is being reorganised around where state actually lives and who is accountable for it. Vendors moved orchestration decisions into the model itself (Anthropic's dynamic workflows, Microsoft's distributed skills over MCP), while researchers and practitioners simultaneously produced measured evidence that the environment outside the model — tool reliability, backend database state, sandbox snapshots, execution feedback — determines whether an agent actually works. The practical consequence is that harness builders should stop treating the agent loop as the unit of design and start treating observable terminal state as the unit of both evaluation and recovery.
synthesis:
Three strands converged this month that no single source frames together. First, orchestration is being pushed into the model: Anthropic's dynamic workflows let the lead agent write its own multi-agent topology rather than requiring a developer-configured coordinator and roster, and Microsoft's distributed-skills pattern moves specialist instructions into the orchestrator's context instead of spawning a nested agent loop per specialist. Both are vendor-authored and neither carries controlled measurement — Microsoft's own three-pair comparison explicitly disclaims being 'a controlled performance or quality study', and Anthropic's presenters conceded that flows cost 'much more' than a single-agent approach. Second, the measurement side moved in the opposite direction, toward grading the environment rather than the trajectory: ThinkingBox grades terminal backend state and finds that two-thirds of failures still terminated cleanly with a state-changing tool call and no final tool error. Third, the recovery and reliability layer got concrete: RATED shows that tool retrieval reranked on live execution feedback cuts fault selection from 86.2% to 2.9% under injected outages, and the Daytona/Waterloo snapshot paper shows that full-machine restoration only beats a git diff when progress lives outside the repository.

What our analysis adds is the constraint shared across all of these: each development is an answer to the question 'what state does the next step need, and where is it kept?' Anthropic's flows answer it with a shared filesystem between subagents. Microsoft's skills answer it by relocating instructions into one context. RATED answers it with a per-tool bandit updated from execution outcomes. ThinkingBox answers it by refusing to accept any answer that isn't visible in the database. The snapshot paper answers it by showing that the answer is task-dependent — on file-centric tasks source state suffices, on a task whose progress lives in a SQLite file it does not. Harness builders who have been treating context management as a prompt-assembly problem should read this month as evidence that it is increasingly a state-ownership problem.
limitations: The orchestration developments (dynamic workflows, distributed skills, Managed Deep Agents, Foundry isolation) are all vendor-sourced and none carry independent measurement; Microsoft's own comparison is three request pairs on one demo and it says so. The measured results that do exist (RATED, ThinkingBox, the snapshot paper, Naresh Jain's experiment (on martinfowler.com)) are each single studies on specific task distributions, and ThinkingBox's tasks are explicitly 'synthetic reconstruction'. Missing perspectives: open-source maintainers of competing orchestration frameworks, enterprise operators running these patterns at scale for more than a quarter, and non-US builders. We have no independent replication of any vendor claim here.

claims.statement: Anthropic announced 'dynamic workflows', where the lead agent writes its own orchestration program rather than the developer configuring a coordinator and subagent roster.

locator.quote: The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow. Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents.

claims.statement: Anthropic's presenters said the model does not know its budget while running, and that flows cost 'much more' than a single-agent approach in their watchlist-scanner comparison.

locator.quote: Stall replied that the model does not know its budget while running, but that developers can set a session budget.
In the watchlist-scanner comparison, Avilla said flows cost “much more” than a single-agent approach, but were also “much more effective at finding all of the details.”

claims.statement: Microsoft published a competing orchestration pattern in which specialist instructions move into the orchestrator's context rather than running as a separate agent loop, with the author's own three-pair trace comparison showing three model calls for the skills path versus six or seven for the A2A path.

locator.quote: The structural observation is narrower: six, six, and seven model calls across A2A components versus three calls in each skills-advisor run, with skill loading followed immediately by direct MCP operations.
It did not use fewer total tokens. Across three runs, native skills consumed 13,533 observed tokens versus 11,134 for A2A, about 22% more. Fewer model calls did not mean less cumulative context.

claims.statement: The ThinkingBox benchmark grades agents on terminal backend database state and reports that of 79,853 failed attempts across 121,680 valid trials, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error.

locator.quote: In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error.

claims.statement: RATED reports that reranking tool retrieval with a contextual bandit updated from execution feedback reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under a 30% failure injection, at under 1 ms of added latency.

locator.quote: Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference.

claims.statement: A sandbox-snapshot search paper found that full-machine restoration beat source-only restoration only when progress lived outside the repository: on a task whose state sat in a SQLite database, snapshots solved 4/5 attempts while git-diff and clean restarts solved 0/5.

locator.quote: on a custom task whose progress lives in a SQLite database outside git, full snapshots solve 4/5 attempts and source-only restoration solves 0/5

claims.statement: Arize reports that changing one tool description cut Codex's unnecessary skill loads from 51 to zero and lowered a benchmark run's cost from $11.85 to $8.34 with correctness unchanged.

locator.quote: Changing one tool description reduced Codex’s unnecessary skill loads from 51 to zero and lowered the cost of our benchmark run from $11.85 to $8.34. Correctness stayed unchanged on the benchmark.

claims.statement: Across this month's developments the common design question is where state lives and who owns it — vendors answer it with shared filesystems and relocated instructions, while measured research answers it with execution feedback, terminal database state, and environment snapshots.

locator.quote: Stall said the agents share a filesystem and can use it to exchange information, but developers cannot directly instruct one workflow subagent to message another through the API.
A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.
A retry from the original repository loses all of this state, while a source-level checkpoint such as a git diff preserves only the subset represented in files un- der version control.

claims.statement: Microsoft shipped a Foundry hosted-agent isolation model that separates user isolation (whose data may be used) from session isolation (where code and files persist), noting that a hosted session is not a conversation.

locator.quote: A Foundry hosted session is not a conversation. A conversation contains message and tool-call history. A Foundry hosted session contains sandbox compute and persisted files.

title: Which Claims Held Up: Harnesses, Judges, and the Gap Between Passing and Working
question: Which of this month's claims withstand scrutiny, and where are the measured results or their interpretations genuinely in tension?
argument: The strongest results this month are negative or conditional, and they converge on one uncomfortable finding: our standard success signals — passing tests, clean tool calls, a single good run — routinely certify work that did not happen. Where sources appear to disagree about whether harness machinery is worth its cost, the disagreement dissolves into a consistent conditional once you control for model capability and for where state lives; where sources genuinely conflict is on how much to trust an LLM judge and on whether "self-improvement" transfers at all.
synthesis:
Three measured results published within days of each other say the same thing from different angles. Jain ran a behavioral harness against two models and found that for a frontier model the harness changed nothing observable while costing roughly seven times more, but turned a cost-optimised model from 3-of-10 to 10-of-10. ThinkingBox found that pass@1 and 20/20 reliability rank models differently — Kimi-K3 solves the most tasks at least once while Claude Opus 5 solves far more consistently — and that a newer model can raise headline accuracy without adding a single dependable task. The Daytona snapshot paper found that a mechanism which perfectly solves state restoration still loses to plain retry, 6/25 against 17/25, because restoration is not selection. Read together, these are not three contradictory verdicts on harness machinery; they are one conditional: added machinery pays when it supplies information the model or the repository does not already have, and costs when it does not. Jain states this explicitly as a revised hypothesis about when sensors run rather than whether.

The genuine tensions are elsewhere. Arize's own re-run of a published tone experiment shows that the original result was confounded — the 'rude' prompts also contained brevity instructions, and when Arize deleted only those words Opus's apparent 55% saving fell to 15% and GPT-4o's threatening saving vanished. That is a methodological warning aimed directly at anyone running eval comparisons, and it sits uneasily beside the same post's report that an LLM judge's agreement with human annotators moved from 0.43 to 0.48 under a rude wrapper without judging any better. Arize's separate Harbor post reaches the same conclusion from practice: 'The LLM judge looked like the easy part. It was wrong a lot of the time.' Meanwhile MC-EvoBench, which was built specifically to audit whether experience transfers, reports that related experience produced no stable transfer and that its one positive contrast hinged on a single seed with all intervals including zero — a direct, measured counterweight to the industry's confidence in memory-driven self-improvement. Our reading is that the field currently has much better tooling for making agents do more than for establishing that they did it, and that the evidence base for memory and self-improvement is substantially weaker than the evidence base for tool reliability and state restoration.
limitations: Jain's experiment is ten paired runs on one greenfield Java service with an unusually detailed brief, and he says so; it cannot separate the contributions of guides versus sensors because they were added together. ThinkingBox's tasks are synthetic reconstructions and its costs are list-price estimates, not invoices. MC-EvoBench's negative transfer finding rests on five seeds per probe with wide intervals, uses one reference method, and its own authors note that most runs ended before crafting sticks, so later capabilities were never observed — the absence of transfer may partly be an absence of measurement. Arize's tone work is commercially affiliated (they sell eval tooling) even though the method is checkable. None of these has been independently replicated. Missing: security researchers' view on whether state-grading benchmarks can be gamed, and any enterprise operator reporting these effects at production scale.

claims.statement: Naresh Jain (writing on martinfowler.com) reports that a behavioral harness made no observable difference to a frontier model's acceptance rate (10/10 either way) while using about 10.5 times as many tokens and costing about 7 times more.

locator.quote: For GPT-6 Sol, the harness used about 10.5 times as many tokens, took nearly 3 times as long, and cost about 7 times more, yet both conditions succeeded in all 10 runs.

claims.statement: The same experiment found the harness took a cost-optimized model from 3 of 10 accepted runs to 10 of 10, at 33% lower cost per run than the unharnessed frontier model.

locator.quote: But a cost-optimized model, GPT-6 Luna, succeeded in only 3 of 10 unharnessed runs and all 10 with the harness. While adding the harness increased token usage and runtime for Luna, the harnessed Luna runs achieved the same 10-for-10 reliability as GPT-6 Sol while costing 33% less per run ($0.273 vs $0.406).

claims.statement: ThinkingBox reports that single-attempt accuracy and every-attempt reliability rank models differently: Kimi-K3 solves 93.89% of tasks at least once but only 13.41% on all 20 attempts, while Claude Opus 5 solves fewer at least once but 47.53% consistently.

locator.quote: Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

claims.statement: ThinkingBox also reports that a newer model raised headline accuracy without adding any dependable tasks: Claude Opus 5.5 scored higher than Opus 5 on average yet passed exactly the same 241 tasks on all 20 attempts.

locator.quote: It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

claims.statement: The snapshot-search paper's own pre-registered comparison refuted its hypothesis: independent retry solved 17/25 task-seeds while snapshot branching solved 6/25 under a matched token budget.

locator.quote: and independent retry. On our pre- registered harder Terminal-Bench subset, retry solves 17/25 tasks while snapshot-based search solves 6/25, establishing that reliable restoration alone is not suffi- cient to improve

claims.statement: Arize's re-run of a published tone experiment found the original comparison confounded tone with brevity instructions; deleting only the brevity words cut Opus's apparent 55% saving to 15% and eliminated GPT-4o's threatening saving entirely.

locator.quote: I ran it again with only the brevity words deleted, against a baseline with no prefix at all, and most of the rudeness discount vanished. Opus’s very rude saving fell from 55% to 15%. GPT-4o’s threatening saving went from 22% to nothing.

claims.statement: Two independent Arize posts converge on LLM judges being the weak link: one reports the judge 'was wrong a lot of the time' because of naming inconsistencies, the other reports a cited study finding tone shifts a judge's severity rather than its judgement.

locator.quote: The LLM judge looked like the easy part. It was wrong a lot of the time. TRAIL calls the same tool page_down in one place and PageDownTool in another, so a correct reply could be graded against the wrong spelling.

it looked “more consistent with a shift in the judge’s severity operating point—its overall scoring leniency—than with improved judgment.” They flag tone as “a potential validity threat when absolute relevance labels matter.”

claims.statement: MC-EvoBench, built to audit experience-driven self-improvement, reports that related experience yielded no stable transfer, with its one positive contrast driven by a single seed and all intervals including zero.

locator.quote: while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero.

claims.statement: Where sources appear to disagree about whether harness machinery pays for itself, the disagreement resolves into a shared conditional: added machinery helps only when it supplies information the model or the repository does not already have.

locator.quote: What changes with model capability is not whether independent sensors are needed, but when they run.

It matters most when important progress lives outside the repository, such as in databases, installed packages, running services, generated artifacts, or other machine state that cannot be recovered from Git or source files alone.
Loading a whole provider avoids a separate per-tool loading step but supplies schemas that may not all be used; a smaller initial context is not automatically a faster or cheaper conversation.

title: What To Build Next: State Ownership, Staged Autonomy, and the Audit Trail You Don't Have Yet
question: Given what changed and what held up, what should harness builders do differently now, and what should they watch over the next quarter?
argument: The practical mandate emerging from this month is to make your harness produce evidence by default: grade on terminal state rather than trajectory, log enough to reconstruct a historical decision, and gate autonomy on measured override behaviour rather than on a passing demo. The forces pushing this are not only engineering — the EU AI Act's December 2027 high-risk deadline turns logging, retention and human oversight into build requirements — but the cheapest version of compliance is also the version that makes agents debuggable, which means the two agendas can be served by one investment.
synthesis:
Piece 01 established that state ownership is the shared design question; piece 02 established that our success signals routinely certify work that did not happen. The implication for builders is specific and actionable. First, the evidence layer: Gayle's due-diligence framing — preserve the input prompts, model version, configuration, output, reviewer and action, because 'calling the model again later may produce a different answer' — is the same requirement the EU AI Act imposes under Articles 12, 19 and 26(6), and the same requirement ThinkingBox's grading method implies. One logging design satisfies all three. Second, the autonomy layer: Grant's four-stage ladder (shadow, supervised draft, exception ensemble, exceptions only) gives the staging that Jain's conditional implies — run sensors continuously where unaided outcomes are inconsistent, run them as a final gate where they are not. Grant adds the non-obvious warning that practitioners should internalise: once review moves to exceptions only, 'your biggest vulnerability is what the agent failed to flag', and a falling override rate may mean the depth of review has slipped rather than that the agent improved. That is exactly the failure mode ThinkingBox's clean-termination statistic describes, arriving from a governance direction rather than a benchmark one.

What we would add beyond any single source is a caution about the economics. Jellyfish's measured data says AI is about 2.5% of the cost of producing a merged PR and that cost per merged PR fell 26% over a year — a genuine argument for spending more. But Abelhad's due-diligence checks say the honest denominator must include 'operators, reviewer reviewers, trainers, escalation and rework', and Grant's ladder says the reviewer burden is precisely what you are trying to reduce at stage four. These are not in conflict, but they constrain each other: the case for spending more on tokens weakens exactly to the degree that you are paying humans to compensate for unverified output. Our interpretation is that the teams best positioned over the next two quarters are those who invest in the evidence layer first, because it is the only thing that lets them tell the difference.
limitations: The autonomy ladder and the due-diligence checks are practitioner frameworks presented without quantitative validation; neither Grant nor Abelhad reports a measured outcome from applying them. The Jellyfish figures are observational telemetry from a vendor that sells workflow analytics, and their own slide concedes that revert-rate deltas are 'slightly below the noise in the data'. The EU AI Act guidance is vendor-authored by Arize, which sells the tracing stack it positions as compliance evidence, and the deadlines have already moved once. The strongest counterargument to this whole piece is that heavy evidence infrastructure is itself a cost that may not pay back for teams whose agents are low-consequence; nothing here measures that break-even point. Missing perspectives: non-EU regulators, open-source maintainers who cannot fund an evidence layer, and any operator who has run a staged-autonomy ladder to stage four and reported what they found.

claims.statement: A practitioner speaking on deployment in regulated environments advises preserving the input prompts, model version, configuration, output, reviewer and action, because re-calling the model later may produce a different answer.

The EU AI Act's high-risk obligations, which Arize summarises as largely engineering work including automatic logs, six months of retention, human oversight and post-market monitoring, take effect on 2 December 2027.

locator.quote: Most high-risk obligations are engineering work. Automatic logs, six months of retention, human oversight, post-market monitoring, incident handling, and explanations of decisions are things you build. Most of them are already good practice for running agents in production.

The high-risk deadline is 2 December 2027, and transparency duties already apply. The dates have moved once already because the work is hard to put in place. Start now rather than betting on another move.

claims.statement: A practitioner proposes a four-stage autonomy ladder and warns that at the exceptions-only stage the biggest vulnerability is what the agent failed to flag, and that a falling override rate may indicate review depth has slipped rather than improvement.

Jellyfish reports from engineering workflow data joined with AI telemetry that AI is about 2.5% of the intelligence cost of producing a merged PR, and that the dollar cost of a merged PR fell 26% over a year across 83% of companies studied.

A due-diligence practitioner argues that automation claims must net out everyone whose work exists because of AI — operators, reviewers, trainers, escalation and rework — and distinguishes 'AI attributed' from genuinely autonomous completion.

The case for spending more on tokens and the case for staged autonomy constrain each other: cost-per-unit-of-work improvements only hold if the human verification burden they displace is counted honestly, which is precisely what exception-only review makes hard to observe.
Practitioners are already building narrow harness workarounds to keep secrets out of model context, such as a separate web editor over Tailscale so credentials never round-trip through the LLM.

locator.quote: I was working on a project from my phone using Codex Remote when I found myself wanting to edit a credentials file without round-tripping those credentials through the LLM itself.

claims.statement: Watch red-teaming of cross-service tool compositions: X-AgentRed reports 1.77x the harmful path rate of STAC and 2.99x its tool coverage across four frontier agents, suggesting harmful outcomes arise from benign requests composing across services.

locator.quote: Across four frontier agentic models, X-AgentRed achieves \(1.77\times\) the harmful path rate of STAC and explores a more diverse set of tools, yielding \(2.99\times\) the tool coverage on average.

claims.statement: Watch the MCP tool-surface problem: a practitioner reports AWS has roughly 16,000 APIs, too many to model as tools, pushing them toward code-mode execution that is itself hard for humans to review.
